questions.x: The finding runs the other way: fear is inflated, driven by zero-sum framing and feeling powerless, which is why many candidates never ask. Treating the talk as joint problem-solving is the remedy the article suggests, not the cause of the error.

questions.t: In a 2025 field experiment with U.S. tech job seekers, a short encouragement message raised the share who countered their offer to 61%, against 54% in the control group.
questions.f: In a 2025 field experiment with U.S. tech job seekers, a deep discount on paid negotiation coaching raised the share who countered their offer to 61%, against 54% in the control group.
questions.x: Cullen, Pakzad-Hurson and Perez-Truglia found encouragement moved behaviour while cheap coaching did not change how many negotiated. That points to beliefs about risk, not missing skills, as the main barrier.

questions.topic: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
questions.t: In Weger and colleagues' 2014 first-conversation experiment, a partner who offered advice was rated about as socially attractive and satisfying to talk to as one who used active listening.
questions.f: In Weger and colleagues' 2014 first-conversation experiment, a partner who offered advice was rated less socially attractive and less satisfying to talk to than one who used active listening.
questions.x: Active listening beat bare acknowledgement on liking and satisfaction, but not advice. Its distinct payoff was making people feel understood, so reflecting back is not a general boost to how others see you.

questions.topic: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
questions.t: Weger and colleagues trace active listening to Carl Rogers's 1951 account of empathic listening in therapy, and credit Thomas Gordon with turning it into a teachable method.
questions.f: Weger and colleagues trace active listening to Thomas Gordon's 1951 account of empathic listening in therapy, and credit Carl Rogers with turning it into a teachable method.
questions.x: Rogers supplied the therapeutic idea of empathic listening; Gordon later packaged it as a method people could be trained in. The false version swaps their roles.

questions.topic: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
questions.t: One limit of Weger and colleagues' 2014 experiment is that the confederates who used active listening received far more training than the confederates in the other conditions.
questions.f: One limit of Weger and colleagues' 2014 experiment is that the confederates who gave advice received far more training than the confederates using active listening.
questions.x: The active-listening confederates were trained much longer, which could favour that condition. Along with small effects, a student sample and no direct replication, it is why the result is rated mixed.

questions.t: Drafting a culture assimilator episode for her team, a lead writes, "The supplier stayed quiet in the review because he was embarrassed about the delay." She has broken the rule to describe the scene and leave the reason out.
questions.f: Drafting a culture assimilator episode for her team, a lead writes, "The supplier stayed quiet in the review because he was embarrassed about the delay." She has broken the rule to validate each explanation with insiders.
questions.x: Writing the cause into the scene hands learners the answer, so they never practise generating and testing explanations. Insider validation is a separate step that checks which offered explanation locals would accept; the problem here is the description itself.

questions.t: When building a culture assimilator for your team, keep only the episodes whose correct explanation members of the other culture broadly agree on.
questions.f: When building a culture assimilator for your team, keep only the episodes whose correct explanation your team's most experienced expatriate managers agree on.
questions.x: The method aims at explaining behaviour the way the other culture would, so insiders of that culture must confirm each answer. Outsiders, however experienced, can share the very misreading the episode is meant to correct.

questions.t: The culture assimilator came out of 1960s work by Fred Fiedler, Harry Triandis and colleagues, and was first tested with US military, Peace Corps and adviser groups.
questions.f: The culture assimilator came out of 1990s work by Dharm Bhawuk and colleagues, and was first tested with US business students preparing for exchange programmes.
questions.x: Fiedler and Triandis developed the method at Illinois and Washington in the 1960s. Bhawuk came later and built a theory-based version organised around individualism and collectivism.

questions.t: For the third sprint running, a designer drops her own accessibility requirements as soon as the product manager pushes back, saying, "Fine, your call." In Thomas-Kilmann terms she is accommodating: unassertive and cooperative.
questions.f: For the third sprint running, a designer drops her own accessibility requirements as soon as the product manager pushes back, saying, "Fine, your call." In Thomas-Kilmann terms she is avoiding: unassertive and uncooperative.
questions.x: She yields to the other person's concerns rather than sidestepping the issue, which is accommodating; done habitually it breeds resentment. Avoiding would mean postponing or dodging the disagreement, serving neither side's concerns.

questions.t: Facing an unfamiliar negotiator, test them on a small issue first, checking whether they reciprocate concessions and share information, then adapt your approach to what you see.
questions.f: Facing an unfamiliar negotiator, share all your information on the first issue to model collaboration, so they convert to a collaborative style.
questions.x: People assume others share their conflict style, and a cooperative negotiator who discloses freely can be exploited by a competitor. Probing on small issues lets you adapt rather than trying to convert their style.

questions.t: Because each TKI item makes you choose one mode over another, a high score on a mode shows a relative preference, not an absolute amount of that behaviour.
questions.f: Because each TKI item rates a mode on its own scale, a high score on a mode shows an absolute amount of that behaviour, comparable across people.
questions.x: The TKI's 30 forced-choice pairs trade modes against each other, so scores describe how a person ranks the modes. Reading them as absolute amounts, or as a fixed type, is a common misuse.

questions.t: Working out which "Friday" a handover note means is near-side pragmatics: the context needed to fix what was said at all.
questions.f: Working out which "Friday" a handover note means is far-side pragmatics: the speech act performed and the implications beyond the words.
questions.x: Resolving references like "you", "this" or "Friday" is needed just to know what was said, which is the near side. Far-side pragmatics comes after, as in hearing a director's "quick suggestion" as an instruction.

questions.t: A new analyst emails a CFO she has never met, "Hey, need the Q3 numbers asap, thx," and the CFO is put off. In Jenny Thomas's terms that is sociopragmatic failure, misjudging the power and distance of the relationship.
questions.f: A new analyst emails a CFO she has never met, "Hey, need the Q3 numbers asap, thx," and the CFO is put off. In Jenny Thomas's terms that is pragmalinguistic failure, using a form that carries a different force than intended.
questions.x: The request itself is clear; what misfires is a casual register that ignores the status gap, which is the sociopragmatic kind. Pragmalinguistic failure is when the form conveys the wrong force, like hearing "Would you like to read?" as a question about preference.

questions.t: In Hofweber and Jaworska's 2022 study of internal emails at a multinational insurer, 62% of requests were direct, mostly "please" plus an imperative.
questions.f: In Hofweber and Jaworska's 2022 study of internal emails at a multinational insurer, only 38% of requests were direct, with most phrased as "could you…?"
questions.x: Most requests were direct, and nearly all the indirect ones used the "could you…?" form. Directness also tracked senders' first language, so a blunt request is often a habit rather than rudeness.

questions.t: Pitching a shared on-call rota, a team lead tells the directors: "Picture a quarter where nobody gets paged three nights running and incidents still close within an hour." In Monroe's sequence, that is the visualization step.
questions.f: Pitching a shared on-call rota, a team lead tells the directors: "Picture a quarter where nobody gets paged three nights running and incidents still close within an hour." In Monroe's sequence, that is the satisfaction step.
questions.x: She is painting the concrete future once the solution is in place, which is visualization. Satisfaction would be explaining the rota itself, showing it works and answering the strongest objection.

questions.t: Proposing a pilot to senior leaders who expect the conclusion first, state your ask at the start and use Monroe's need, solution and visualization steps as the body that supports it.
questions.f: Proposing a pilot to senior leaders who expect the conclusion first, keep Monroe's canonical order and hold the ask for the close, since that order is what makes the sequence persuasive.
questions.x: For answer-first readers a solution held back to the end can read as stalling, and the one controlled test found the canonical order is not the active ingredient. The steps still work as a checklist of what to cover.

questions.t: In Micciche, Pryor and Butler's 2000 test, an argument for a parking-fee rise changed attitudes no more with its five steps in Monroe's order than in reverse or random order.
questions.f: In Micciche, Pryor and Butler's 2000 test, an argument for a parking-fee rise changed attitudes clearly more with its five steps in Monroe's order than in reverse or random order.
questions.x: This small written-message study is the only controlled test, and it found no persuasive edge for the canonical order. The sequence's status is contested, so treat it as a coverage checklist rather than a proven formula.

questions.t: The CFO asks a programme manager whether the project will overrun. She lists every open risk, apologises twice and ends, "Honestly, it's hard to say." Her answer undercuts presence by showing hedging rather than a clear call under pressure.
questions.f: The CFO asks a programme manager whether the project will overrun. She lists every open risk, apologises twice and ends, "Honestly, it's hard to say." Her answer builds presence by showing the listen-to-learn style executives now prefer.
questions.x: Confidence under pressure and decisiveness lead the gravitas pillar, and she offers neither. Listen-to-learn means asking and drawing others in, not withholding a judgement; a pause, her best estimate and the decision she needs would read far better.

questions.t: When a manager says you need "more presence", ask what they saw you do, then pick two or three observable behaviours to practise and get feedback on.
questions.f: When a manager says you need "more presence", pick a senior leader everyone admires and copy their speaking style and manner as closely as you can.
questions.x: Vague presence feedback only becomes usable once it is turned into specific behaviours you can rehearse. Copying someone else's style works against the authenticity now valued; the aim is to show your own judgement more clearly.

questions.t: More charisma is not always better: in Vergauwe and colleagues' study of several hundred leaders, those with very high charismatic personality were rated weaker on operational follow-through.
questions.f: More charisma is always better: in Vergauwe and colleagues' study of several hundred leaders, those with very high charismatic personality were rated strongest on operational follow-through.
questions.x: The link between charisma and rated effectiveness was curvilinear, so beyond a point more charisma hurt on getting things done. It is a caution against treating presence as maximum charisma, especially since the construct itself rests mostly on surveys and interviews.

questions.t: Reviewing a consultant's muddled deck, a manager says, "Next time, sketch the storyline on sticky notes before you open the slides." In Hattie and Timperley's model that is process-level feedback.
questions.f: Reviewing a consultant's muddled deck, a manager says, "Next time, sketch the storyline on sticky notes before you open the slides." In Hattie and Timperley's model that is task-level feedback.
questions.x: The comment targets the method that produced the deck, which is the process level. Task-level feedback would say what is right, wrong or missing in this particular deck, such as "slide 4 has no conclusion."

questions.t: When a report's draft misses the mark, start by confirming the goal you both hold for it, then compare the draft with that goal and name the next step.
questions.f: When a report's draft misses the mark, start by listing everything that's off, then name the next step, and agree what the goal was only at the end.
questions.x: The model's order is where am I going, how am I going, where to next. Comments help only when the person knows the target, and missing goals are a common reason feedback fails.

questions.t: A 2020 meta-analysis co-authored by Hattie backed the idea that more informative feedback works better, but it could not test the model's claim that praise of the person is the least effective level.
questions.f: A 2020 meta-analysis co-authored by Hattie backed the idea that more informative feedback works better, and it confirmed the model's claim that praise of the person is the least effective level.
questions.x: The 2020 review found information-rich feedback outperformed bare rewards or punishments, but it could not code the four levels at all. So the self-level claim remains untested there, part of why the model's status is mixed.

questions.t: After a client spends ten minutes on a call listing frustrations, the account manager says, "So three things: invoices arrive late, the portal times out at month-end, and you're unsure who your new contact is. Did I miss anything?" That is summarizing.
questions.f: After a client spends ten minutes on a call listing frustrations, the account manager says, "So three things: invoices arrive late, the portal times out at month-end, and you're unsure who your new contact is. Did I miss anything?" That is paraphrasing.
questions.x: The reply gathers several points from a long stretch of talk into one organised statement and invites correction, which is a summary. A paraphrase restates a single point; scope is what separates them.

questions.t: When summarizing a colleague's concerns, keep your own view and proposed fix out of the summary, and raise them only once they have confirmed or corrected it.
questions.f: When summarizing a colleague's concerns, fold your own view and proposed fix into the summary, so they can confirm both your reading and your plan at once.
questions.x: A summary is a clarifying move that tests understanding; adding your position turns the check into an argument or a proposal. Confirm their version first, then use it as the bridge to solutions.

questions.t: In Rackham and Carlisle's 1978 observations of real negotiations, skilled negotiators spent about 7.5% of their behaviour summarizing, against about 4.2% for average negotiators.
questions.f: In Rackham and Carlisle's 1978 observations of real negotiations, skilled negotiators spent about 4.2% of their behaviour summarizing, against about 7.5% for average negotiators.
questions.x: Skilled negotiators summarized nearly twice as often. The data are observational, so they show an association rather than proof that summarizing causes better deals, and summarizing overall is rated only practitioner-level evidence.

questions.t: A project lead's recap lists "Marketing to follow up on the pricing page" and "We'll look into the API errors." Those are owners by implication: neither action names one responsible person or a date.
questions.f: A project lead's recap lists "Marketing to follow up on the pricing page" and "We'll look into the API errors." That is a transcript recap: a blow-by-blow account that buries the decisions.
questions.x: The tell is "marketing" and "we" in place of a named person, and no due date. A transcript recap is the opposite problem, too much narrative; the fix here is one owner, a verb-first task and a deadline per line.

questions.t: Before a meeting ends, read the decisions and actions aloud and have each owner confirm their task and date in the room, so nobody first learns of a task from the recap.
questions.f: After a meeting, send the recap with each new task assigned and let owners raise any objections by reply, so the meeting can end on time.
questions.x: A spoken read-back lets people object before the record is fixed and gets commitments out loud. Surprise assignments that first appear in the email tend to invite pushback.

questions.t: The case for owner-task-date recaps rests mostly on expert consensus; the implementation-intentions research cited for it studied individuals' own if-then plans, not team action lists.
questions.f: The case for owner-task-date recaps rests mostly on trials comparing teams that send recaps with teams that don't, which found clearly better follow-through.
questions.x: No studies directly compare teams with and without recaps, so the practice is rated practitioner. Goal-setting research on concrete when-and-how plans offers a plausible mechanism, not proof that recaps work.

questions.t: Before a board update, a manager runs a speech-analysis tool that flags her pace, flat pitch and fillers, and she tries to fix all three in one evening's practice. That is chasing every metric.
questions.f: Before a board update, a manager runs a speech-analysis tool that flags her pace, flat pitch and fillers, and she tries to fix all three in one evening's practice. That is over-correcting.
questions.x: Working on every flagged reading at once dilutes the practice; the published training picked one parameter and drilled it until it shifted. Over-correcting is a different mistake: pushing one reading so far that the voice stops sounding natural.

questions.t: When training a flat voice against a pitch meter, drill the sentences that carry the key points of your own upcoming talk, rather than a set of generic practice sentences.
questions.f: When training a flat voice against a pitch meter, drill a set of generic practice sentences, rather than the sentences that carry the key points of your own upcoming talk.
questions.x: Hincks and Edlund had each student repeat lines pulled from their own baseline presentation, and the gain carried over to the real talk. Your own sentences also let you decide which word in each should stand out.

questions.t: In Hincks and Edlund's 2009 pitch-meter study, trainees clearly widened their pitch variation, yet expert listeners heard only slight gains in liveliness and no reliable gain in naturalness.
questions.f: In Hincks and Edlund's 2009 pitch-meter study, trainees clearly widened their pitch variation, and expert listeners heard large gains in liveliness and a reliable gain in naturalness.
questions.x: The acoustic measure moved much more than listeners' impressions did, and the sample was tiny, so the evidence is rated mixed. A better reading on the meter is not proof of a better presenter; check the result by ear.

questions.t: Halfway through a client briefing on a delayed rollout, the account lead says, "So, to recap this part: one delay came from the vendor and one from the audit, and both are now fixed." That is an internal summary.
questions.f: Halfway through a client briefing on a delayed rollout, the account lead says, "So, to recap this part: one delay came from the vendor and one from the audit, and both are now fixed." That is an internal preview.
questions.x: The line looks back and recaps what was just covered, which makes it an internal summary. An internal preview looks forward and announces what is coming next, such as "Now the new date and the one risk to it."

questions.t: When moving between points in a talk, say a transition that closes one point and names the next, such as "That's the cost; now the timeline," rather than just "Moving on."
questions.f: When moving between points in a talk, keep transitions to a quick "Moving on" or "Next slide," rather than spending a sentence on what was just said and what comes next.
questions.x: "Moving on" tells listeners only that something changed, not how the new point relates to the last one. Naming both lets someone who drifted for a minute rejoin the structure.

questions.t: A 2020 meta-analysis of 29 experiments found that cues signalling structure in multimedia learning gave a modest overall benefit (d = 0.38), with large variation between studies.
questions.f: A 2020 meta-analysis of 29 experiments found that cues signalling structure in multimedia learning gave a large, consistent benefit (d = 0.83), with little variation between studies.
questions.x: The pooled effect was moderate and varied widely, with stronger effects in better-controlled designs. Most of this evidence comes from classrooms, so its size in short workplace briefings is an extrapolation.

questions.t: In a one-on-one, after a report has listed three ways to clear her review backlog, her manager asks, "Which will you start with, and when shall we check how it went?" In GROW, that question opens the Will stage.
questions.f: In a one-on-one, after a report has listed three ways to clear her review backlog, her manager asks, "Which will you start with, and when shall we check how it went?" In GROW, that question opens the Options stage.
questions.x: Options is where routes are generated; she has already listed three. Asking her to choose one, name a first step and set a review point is Will, or Way forward.

questions.t: When coaching a report through GROW, ask for her options first and add your own idea only after hers, labelled as one option among several.
questions.f: When coaching a report through GROW, lead with your own recommended option so she has a strong starting point, then ask what else she could try.
questions.x: Putting your idea first anchors her and quietly hands ownership back to you, which GROW is meant to avoid. You can still contribute, but after her ideas and as one choice rather than the answer.

questions.t: In a 2015 randomised replication, solution-focused coaching questions raised students' self-efficacy and planned action steps more than problem-focused questions about causes and history.
questions.f: In a 2015 randomised replication, problem-focused coaching questions about causes and history raised students' self-efficacy and planned action steps more than solution-focused questions.
questions.x: This supports keeping GROW's Reality stage brief and moving to what would be better. GROW itself rests on practitioner consensus; it is the questioning stance, not the model, that has controlled evidence.

questions.t: A team lead posts one unbroken twelve-line paragraph in a ticket, with three separate requests for three people spread through it. Only the first request gets done. That is a wall of text: nothing guides the scanning eye to the later asks.
questions.f: A team lead posts one unbroken twelve-line paragraph in a ticket, with three separate requests for three people spread through it. Only the first request gets done. That is information overload: the team simply receives too many messages to keep up.
questions.x: The failure sits inside one message: dense, unformatted text, so scanners act on the top and miss the rest. Information overload describes too much incoming communication overall; the fix here is one line per request, each with an owner.

questions.t: In a long status email, bold only the one or two phrases readers must not miss, such as a deadline, because highlighting one passage makes the rest less likely to be read.
questions.f: In a long status email, bold every sentence that carries an important detail, because highlighting more passages makes each of them more likely to be read.
questions.x: Emphasis works by contrast, and highlighted text draws attention away from everything else. Bolding many sentences erodes that contrast, so save it for the few phrases that must be seen.

questions.t: In a 2005 Wichita State study, an enhanced layout with headers and indentation left reading speed and comprehension unchanged, though readers found it more satisfying and less tiring.
questions.f: In a 2005 Wichita State study, an enhanced layout with headers and indentation clearly improved comprehension, though readers found it no more satisfying or less tiring.
questions.x: Breaking up text mainly helps readers find things and feel less worn out; it does not by itself make unclear content understood. The false version swaps which outcome moved.

questions.t: A contractor quotes a client a $900 day rate. The client says nothing for a few seconds, and the contractor adds, "I could probably do $820." She has filled the silence with a unilateral concession before the client moved.
questions.f: A contractor quotes a client a $900 day rate. The client says nothing for a few seconds, and the contractor adds, "I could probably do $820." She has made a contingent concession tied to the client's next move.
questions.x: Nothing was asked in return and the client had not countered, so the drop is unilateral, prompted only by discomfort with silence. A contingent concession names a specific action the other side must take, such as a longer engagement.

questions.t: If you want to tell a vendor firmly that you have other options, line up a genuine alternative quote before the meeting, so the strong statement is also true.
questions.f: If you want to tell a vendor firmly that you have other options, mention a competing quote you could plausibly get, since bluffing about alternatives is normal hard bargaining.
questions.x: Declining to reveal your bottom line is fair, but inventing an offer risks reputation and future deals and can be illegal. The ethical move is to change the facts first, for example by getting real quotes or capping your authority.

questions.t: In Korobkin and Doherty's 2009 settlement simulations, the strongest predictor of who captured more of the surplus was how accurately each side estimated the other's reservation price.
questions.f: In Korobkin and Doherty's 2009 settlement simulations, the strongest predictor of who captured more of the surplus was how large each side's first offer was.
questions.x: First-offer size mattered, but it came after the accuracy of estimating the counterpart's bottom line. The lesson is to research and probe the other side's walk-away point before you start dividing value.

questions.t: A support manager opens a client-escalation huddle sighing and muttering, "This is a disaster." Within minutes her team is snapping at each other, though nobody mentions her tone. That is emotional contagion.
questions.f: A support manager opens a client-escalation huddle sighing and muttering, "This is a disaster." Within minutes her team is snapping at each other, though nobody mentions her tone. That is low psychological safety.
questions.x: Her irritation spreads to the group without anyone noticing it happen, which is mood transfer; leaders are an especially strong source because people watch them. Psychological safety is about whether people dare to speak up or admit mistakes, which this exchange does not show.

questions.t: Before a tense one-on-one, check and settle your own mood first, because your face, voice and posture carry it to the other person even when your words stay neutral.
questions.f: Before a tense one-on-one, check that your wording is neutral, because as long as your words stay neutral your mood stays with you rather than passing to the other person.
questions.x: In Barsade's experiment the confederate changed only his nonverbal displays, yet the group's mood shifted. This is reasoned practice drawn from the mechanism rather than a tested protocol, but neutral words alone do not contain a mood.

questions.t: Hess and Fischer's 2013 review found people mimic the emotions of friends and allies far more than those of rivals, which undercuts the idea that emotional mimicry is an automatic motor copy.
questions.f: Hess and Fischer's 2013 review found people mimic the emotions of rivals as readily as those of friends and allies, which supports the idea that emotional mimicry is an automatic motor copy.
questions.x: Mimicry depends on the relationship, which is why the mechanism is contested and the evidence rated mixed. In practice, enthusiasm may not spread to a sceptical or competing counterpart.

questions.t: Writing a first email to a client's procurement lead she has never met, an account manager closes with "Looking forward to working together :)". In formal first contacts like this, smileys tend to lower how competent the sender seems.
questions.f: Writing a first email to a client's procurement lead she has never met, an account manager closes with "Looking forward to working together :)". In formal first contacts like this, smileys tend to raise warmth with no cost to perceived competence.
questions.x: Glikson and colleagues found smileys in a work email to an unknown contact lowered perceived competence, and recipients shared less in reply. The warmth-without-cost result held only in informal settings.

questions.t: When telling a teammate in chat that their deck needs major rework, state the problem and the next step in plain words rather than adding a smiley to soften it.
questions.f: When telling a teammate in chat that their deck needs major rework, keep it short and add a smiley at the end, since a positive emoji cushions criticism.
questions.x: Positive emoji did not soften bad news or criticism in workplace messages and can read as insincere. Carry the reassurance and the next step in words instead.

questions.t: In a 2016 University of Minnesota study, readers disagreed about whether a single emoji's sentiment was positive, neutral or negative about a quarter of the time.
questions.f: In a 2016 University of Minnesota study, readers disagreed about whether a single emoji's sentiment was positive, neutral or negative about three-quarters of the time.
questions.x: Disagreement came up in roughly one case in four, and grew when readers saw different platforms' renderings. That's why the advice is to pick one common, clearly positive emoji, if any.

questions.t: In their 2001 paper "First offers as anchors", Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler found that whichever side opened, buyer or seller, tended to get the better deal.
questions.f: In their 2001 paper "First offers as anchors", Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler found that whichever side waited for the other to open, buyer or seller, tended to get the better deal.
questions.x: The experiments showed a first-mover advantage, with the opening number strongly predicting the final price, face to face and over email. That turned anchoring into tested negotiation advice.

questions.t: In Galinsky and colleagues' 2008 study, MBA students told to imagine what their counterpart was thinking reached a deal needing a creative solution 76% of the time, versus 39% for controls.
questions.f: In Galinsky and colleagues' 2008 study, MBA students told to imagine what their counterpart was feeling reached a deal needing a creative solution 76% of the time, versus 39% for controls.
questions.x: Thinking about the other side's thoughts, perspective-taking, produced the jump; imagining their feelings, empathy, did no better than controls. The studies used MBA students in simulations of modest size.

questions.t: Galinsky's range of acceptable behavior is the span of conduct others will accept from you before backlash, and he argues that power is what sets how wide it is.
questions.f: Galinsky's range of acceptable behavior is the span of conduct others will accept from you before backlash, and he argues that likeability is what sets how wide it is.
questions.x: In his 2016 talk, power determines how much room you have to speak up; low-power people face backlash sooner. His tips for widening the range, such as offering choices or advocating for others, are practitioner advice rather than a tested intervention.

questions.t: Asking a busy architect to review her schema, a developer writes, "I know you're swamped this week. Could you spare 15 minutes before Friday?" She is protecting his negative face, his wish not to be imposed on.
questions.f: Asking a busy architect to review her schema, a developer writes, "I know you're swamped this week. Could you spare 15 minutes before Friday?" She is protecting his positive face, his wish to be approved of and liked.
questions.x: A request imposes on someone's time and autonomy, so acknowledging the imposition and phrasing it as a question protects negative face. Positive face is about being liked and approved of, which criticism, not a request, mainly threatens.

questions.t: If a senior colleague's figures in a client deck are out of date, message her privately before the rehearsal and offer to swap them in or let her do it.
questions.f: If a senior colleague's figures in a client deck are out of date, point it out during the team rehearsal so the fix is made openly in front of everyone.
questions.x: Choosing a private setting removes the audience that makes losing face costly, and leaving her in control of the fix protects her image while still making the correction clear. A public correction threatens her competence in front of peers.

questions.t: In Oetzel and Ting-Toomey's 2003 four-country survey, concern for one's own face predicted a dominating conflict style, while concern for the other person's face predicted avoiding and integrating.
questions.f: In Oetzel and Ting-Toomey's 2003 four-country survey, concern for the other person's face predicted a dominating conflict style, while concern for one's own face predicted avoiding and integrating.
questions.x: Protecting your own image pushed people to dominate, while protecting the other's image went with avoiding or integrating. The data were self-reported by college students, so treat the link as a tendency, not a rule.

questions.t: De Dreu and Weingart's 2003 meta-analysis found task conflict, not just relationship conflict, was negatively related to team performance and satisfaction, against the textbook claim that it helps.
questions.f: De Dreu and Weingart's 2003 meta-analysis found task conflict reliably improved team performance and satisfaction, while only relationship conflict hurt them.
questions.x: The review contradicted the then-common view that disagreement about the work reliably helps teams. Later work found task conflict is least harmful when it stays separate from personal friction, so substance-only debate is not automatically healthy.

questions.t: Morton Deutsch argued that competitive exchanges tend to escalate while cooperative ones build on themselves, because each kind of relationship reproduces the processes that created it.
questions.f: Morton Deutsch argued that competitive exchanges tend to settle down over time while cooperative ones tend to slide into rivalry, because each kind of relationship wears away the processes that created it.
questions.x: In Deutsch's account, suspicion and deception breed more of the same, as do trust and openness, so a dispute's course is self-reinforcing. That is why protecting cooperative features such as honesty and open information matters early.

questions.t: Charles Osgood's 1962 GRIT proposal sought to reduce tension through small, announced concessions that the other side is invited to reciprocate.
questions.f: Kenneth Boulding's 1962 GRIT proposal sought to reduce tension through small, announced concessions that the other side is invited to reciprocate.
questions.x: GRIT is Osgood's idea. Boulding's landmark contribution the same year was the book Conflict and Defense, a different early work in the field.

questions.t: In a weekly design review where the director usually opens each topic, ask her to hold her view until everyone else has spoken.
questions.f: In a weekly design review where the director usually opens each topic, ask her to state her view first so others have something concrete to react to.
questions.x: Early and frequent speakers gain influence whatever the quality of their input, so a leader who opens anchors the room. Letting the senior person speak last gets the others' views on the table first.

questions.t: In a 2020 study of leaderless groups, the time a member spent talking predicted whether others saw them as a leader, even with intelligence, personality and gender controlled for.
questions.f: In a 2020 study of leaderless groups, the time a member spent talking predicted whether others saw them as a leader, but only because the biggest talkers were also the most intelligent.
questions.x: The effect held after controlling for intelligence, so airtime itself buys influence. That is how lopsided talk rewards whoever speaks first and longest, not whoever knows most.

questions.t: The popular line that two people do over 60% of the talking in a six-person meeting is offered by Leigh Thompson without a named study, so treat it as an illustration, not a measured norm.
questions.f: The popular line that two people do over 60% of the talking in a six-person meeting comes from Woolley and colleagues' 2010 studies, so treat it as a measured norm.
questions.x: Kellogg's page presents the figure with no study behind it. Woolley's 2010 work was about turn-taking equality and a collective intelligence factor, not this airtime statistic.

questions.t: When a junior colleague raises a risk in a team meeting, respond to it promptly as chair, rather than letting a few seconds of silence hang after she speaks.
questions.f: When a junior colleague raises a risk in a team meeting, let a few seconds of silence hang as chair before responding, to show you are weighing it seriously.
questions.x: In the Groningen experiments a brief silence in a group conversation left viewers feeling rejected even when they did not notice it. Right after someone takes a social risk, a gap reads as rejection; save the thinking pause for hard questions put to you.

questions.t: Announcing a reorg, a director opens: "We can keep three teams fighting over one backlog, or give one team the whole thing - I'd choose the second." That opening uses a contrast, one of the charismatic leadership tactics.
questions.f: Announcing a reorg, a director opens: "We can keep three teams fighting over one backlog, or give one team the whole thing - I'd choose the second." That opening uses a metaphor, one of the charismatic leadership tactics.
questions.x: The line sets two options side by side, what we could keep doing versus what we will do, which is the contrast tactic. Nothing is described in terms of something else, so it isn't a metaphor.

questions.t: To get better at charismatic leadership tactics, rehearse on video with feedback and keep practising over several weeks, rather than reading up on the list the night before your talk.
questions.f: To get better at charismatic leadership tactics, read up on the list the night before your talk, rather than spending several weeks rehearsing on video with feedback.
questions.x: The trained gains came from hours of filmed practice and coaching spread over weeks, and the nonverbal tactics in particular were learned by rehearsal, not reading. One-off cramming is a listed mistake.

questions.t: Ernst, Banks and colleagues' 2021 prospective meta-analysis in five countries found charismatic tactics improved performance face to face but had essentially no effect in virtual settings.
questions.f: Ernst, Banks and colleagues' 2021 prospective meta-analysis in five countries found charismatic tactics improved performance most strongly in virtual settings, more than face to face.
questions.x: The pooled virtual effect was close to zero while in-person effects were moderate to large, so a charismatic video or email message needs a clear written summary of the substance rather than relying on the tactics.

questions.t: Giving a budget update, a project lead slows down as she reaches the 18% overrun, says the figure louder, pauses, then makes her request, and the room asks about the number. Her voice is flagging what listeners should remember.
questions.f: Giving a budget update, a project lead slows down as she reaches the 18% overrun, says the figure louder, pauses, then makes her request, and the room asks about the number. Her voice is signalling doubt about the figure.
questions.x: Slowing, a lift in volume and a deliberate silent pause together mark the key point and give listeners time to take it in. A planned pause before a stated request adds weight; it isn't the trailing-off of someone unsure.

questions.t: If your draft talk runs over its slot when you estimate it at about 150 words a minute, cut text rather than plan to speak faster.
questions.f: If your draft talk runs over its slot when you estimate it at about 150 words a minute, plan to speak faster rather than cut text.
questions.x: Rushing is one of the delivery problems listeners complain about most, and good speakers slow down for unfamiliar material and near the close. Trimming the script keeps a rate the room can follow.

questions.t: In Rodero's 2022 experiment with 120 viewers, speeches with a medium amount of pitch variation were rated most effective, ahead of those with few or many variations.
questions.f: In Rodero's 2022 experiment with 120 viewers, speeches with the most pitch variation were rated most effective, ahead of those with a medium amount or few variations.
questions.x: Pitch should move on key words, but the study found a middle level beat both flat and highly varied delivery. It used four actors and 25-second clips, so it may not generalise to long talks.

questions.t: After two stalled talks with the data team lead about a shared deadline, a product lead quietly emails his own VP, who he expects will back him, and doesn't tell the other lead. That is a one-sided escalation, which risks a decision made on partial information.
questions.f: After two stalled talks with the data team lead about a shared deadline, a product lead quietly emails his own VP, who he expects will back him, and doesn't tell the other lead. That is a joint escalation, which gets the decision maker both sides' facts.
questions.x: The tell is that he goes alone to a leader likely to side with him and leaves the other party uninformed. A joint escalation would bring both leads, their positions fairly stated and a record of how they tried to resolve it, to the decision maker together.

questions.t: Once you have escalated a scope dispute and are waiting for the sponsor's decision, keep the team working to the current plan, then confirm the decision in writing to everyone affected when it comes.
questions.f: Once you have escalated a scope dispute and are waiting for the sponsor's decision, pause the affected work so nothing is wasted, then confirm the decision in writing to everyone affected when it comes.
questions.x: Practitioner guidance lists halting work while a decision is pending as a common escalation mistake; the plan in force stays in force until someone with authority changes it. Pausing turns the escalation into a delay of its own.

questions.t: In Park, Im and Keil's 2008 lab experiment, time urgency indirectly raised people's willingness to report project bad news, so stressing how narrow the window to fix a problem is can prompt earlier escalation.
questions.f: In Park, Im and Keil's 2008 lab experiment, time urgency indirectly lowered people's willingness to report project bad news, so stressing how narrow the window to fix a problem tends to delay escalation.
questions.x: The study found urgency pushed reporting up, not down, which is why managers are advised to stress the shrinking window to fix a problem. It is one lab experiment on the mum effect; the escalation practices themselves remain untested practitioner advice.

questions.t: A manager messages an analyst: "Thanks for catching the duplicate invoices on Friday - the client got a clean report and renewed. Next time, though, loop me in sooner." Tacking the correction onto the thanks muddies the recognition.
questions.f: A manager messages an analyst: "Thanks for catching the duplicate invoices on Friday - the client got a clean report and renewed. Next time, though, loop me in sooner." Adding the correction makes the recognition more useful.
questions.x: Recognition works best kept clean: no "but", correction or new request in the same message, or people learn to brace for the catch. Give the thanks on its own and raise the timing point separately.

questions.t: In Grant and Gino's experiments, being thanked made helpers more likely to help again mainly because it made them feel socially valued, not because it made them feel more competent.
questions.f: In Grant and Gino's experiments, being thanked made helpers more likely to help again mainly because it made them feel more competent, not because it made them feel socially valued.
questions.x: The thanks worked through perceived social worth: helpers learned their help was wanted. That is why recognition still matters for confident high performers, who don't need a competence boost.

questions.t: Popular rules that teams need a precise ratio of positive to negative comments, such as 5.6 to 1, trace to a model whose mathematics Brown, Sokal and Friedman showed in 2013 to be unfounded.
questions.f: Popular rules that teams need a precise ratio of positive to negative comments, such as 5.6 to 1, trace to a model that Brown, Sokal and Friedman confirmed in a 2013 replication.
questions.x: Brown, Sokal and Friedman debunked the Fredrickson-Losada positivity-ratio maths, so there is no magic number. Mostly positive interaction is still sound advice; the precise ratio is the myth.

questions.t: A project manager sees that all five engineers opened her email moving the code freeze to Friday and concludes the change has landed. In Weaver's three levels, she has evidence only for the technical level: the message was delivered.
questions.f: A project manager sees that all five engineers opened her email moving the code freeze to Friday and concludes the change has landed. In Weaver's three levels, she has evidence for the semantic level: they took the meaning she intended.
questions.x: Weaver separated delivery, understanding and effect on conduct. An opened email or read receipt proves only delivery; whether engineers read 'Friday' as she meant, or changed their plans, needs a reply or read-back.

questions.t: When a cutover email turns on one date, state that date in both the subject line and the body, adding deliberate redundancy so a skimmed or garbled detail can still be caught.
questions.f: When a cutover email turns on one date, state that date only once, in the body, because repeating it counts as noise that makes the signal harder to decode.
questions.x: In the model, redundancy is the main safeguard against distortion: repeating a key figure, date or owner, or showing it in a second form, lets readers correct an error. Repetition is not noise; noise is what corrupts the signal.

questions.t: Shannon's 1948 paper treated the meaning of messages as irrelevant to its engineering problem, so the model's use for human understanding rests on Warren Weaver's 1949 extension.
questions.f: Weaver's 1949 article treated the meaning of messages as irrelevant to its engineering problem, so the model's use for human understanding rests on Claude Shannon's 1948 extension.
questions.x: Shannon wrote the 1948 engineering paper and set meaning aside; Weaver's 1949 Scientific American piece added the semantic and effectiveness levels. The false version swaps the two men and their dates.

questions.t: Before a team meeting, a lead asks a colleague, "How did your client workshop go?" After a two-word reply, she says, "Mine last week was brilliant - they want a second round." That is boomerasking.
questions.f: Before a team meeting, a lead asks a colleague, "How did your client workshop go?" After a two-word reply, she says, "Mine last week was brilliant - they want a second round." That is reciprocal self-disclosure.
questions.x: The tell is the question used as a launch pad: she asks, barely lets him answer, then answers it herself with a brag. Reciprocal disclosure would alternate her sharing with real interest in his answer.

questions.t: In Yeomans and Brooks's studies, most people expected that asking a question before sharing their own news would make a better impression, yet boomeraskers were judged less sincere and less likeable.
questions.f: In Yeomans and Brooks's studies, people who asked a question before sharing their own news were judged more sincere and likeable, as most of them had expected.
questions.x: Across eight studies, the warm-up question backfired: partners rated boomeraskers as less sincere and less likeable, contrary to what the askers predicted. The cost comes from the question being a pretext.

questions.t: If you notice you asked a colleague a question only to give your own answer, next time just share your news directly, since people prefer plain self-disclosure to a question used as a launch pad.
questions.f: If you notice you asked a colleague a question only to give your own answer, next time ask two warm-up questions before sharing, so your news feels less self-focused.
questions.x: The fix for boomerasking is to drop the pretext: say what you want to share plainly, or ask questions you can't answer yourself and listen to the reply. More warm-up questions only extend the disguise.

questions.t: Opening a client call, the client asks a consultant, "How's your quarter been?" She answers briefly, then replies, "And how's yours been?" In Huang and colleagues' terms, that is a mirror question.
questions.f: Opening a client call, the client asks a consultant, "How's your quarter been?" She answers briefly, then replies, "And how's yours been?" In Huang and colleagues' terms, that is a follow-up question.
questions.x: A mirror question bounces back the question just asked. A follow-up would build on something the client actually said, such as asking about a detail of their answer, which is the kind most tied to liking.

questions.t: When probing a colleague's account of a project, use an expansive probe such as "What did that look like?" when you need breadth, and a targeted one such as "How sure are you?" when you need precision.
questions.f: When probing a colleague's account of a project, use a targeted probe such as "How sure are you?" when you need breadth, and an expansive one such as "What did that look like?" when you need precision.
questions.x: Expansive probes open the answer up and gather more detail; targeted probes pin down one point, such as confidence or how a decision was made. Choose by whether you need range or exactness.

questions.t: Kluger and Malloy's 2019 reanalysis of the speed-dating data found that, for men, asking more questions tended to predict fewer second-date offers, challenging the field part of Huang's work.
questions.f: Kluger and Malloy's 2019 reanalysis of the speed-dating data found that, for men, asking more questions tended to predict more second-date offers, confirming the field part of Huang's work.
questions.x: The reanalysis cut against the original field result and argued a second-date offer isn't the same as liking. The original team replied that the benefits held, so the chat-study effect stands better than the field one.

questions.t: To check a draft for a buried lede, ask a colleague who doesn't know the project to read only the first lines and tell you the point, since unfamiliar readers most need it stated.
questions.f: To check a draft for a buried lede, ask a teammate who knows the project well to read only the first lines and tell you the point, since informed readers spot a missing point fastest.
questions.x: Readers who know the topic infer the main idea anyway, so a teammate will 'find' a point that a newcomer would miss. Testing cold with an unfamiliar reader exposes whether the opening actually states it.

questions.t: In Kieras's 1980 study, stating the main idea up front cut reading time for one unfamiliar technical passage to about 52 seconds, against about 81 seconds without it.
questions.f: In Kieras's 1980 study, stating the main idea up front cut reading time for one unfamiliar technical passage to about 81 seconds, against about 152 seconds without it.
questions.x: The reported gap was roughly 52 versus 81 seconds, and it held for unfamiliar topics; with familiar ones readers worked out the main idea regardless. The false version inflates both times.

questions.t: A 2026 experiment on health journalism found narrative articles produced higher comprehension and interest than inverted-pyramid versions, so putting the point first is not always best for learning.
questions.f: A 2026 experiment on health journalism found inverted-pyramid articles produced higher comprehension and interest than narrative versions, confirming that putting the point first is always best for learning.
questions.x: The narrative versions won on comprehension and interest, which is why the article's evidence status is mixed. Leading with the point matters most for busy readers who must act; a story-first structure can suit writing meant to be read in full.

questions.t: A buyer assumes her vendor wants an early go-live, so she gives up a volume discount to secure the later date she prefers. The vendor wanted the later date too. Missing an issue where both sides want the same outcome is the incompatibility error.
questions.f: A buyer assumes her vendor wants an early go-live, so she gives up a volume discount to secure the later date she prefers. The vendor wanted the later date too. Missing an issue where both sides want the same outcome is anchoring on the first offer.
questions.x: Thompson and Hastie separated the fixed-sum error from the incompatibility error, which is failing to spot issues both sides actually agree on. The tell is that she paid for something the vendor wanted anyway; nobody's opening number drove it, so anchoring does not fit.

questions.t: Before renegotiating a support contract, picture having to explain to your manager how you reached the deal, not just what you won; accountability for the process weakened fixed-pie thinking in experiments.
questions.f: Before renegotiating a support contract, picture having to report to your manager only the final price you won; accountability for the bottom line weakened fixed-pie thinking in experiments.
questions.x: De Dreu and colleagues found that being accountable for how you negotiated raised the motive to be accurate and led to more integrative deals. Focusing only on the number you extract keeps the deal framed as one pie to split.

questions.t: Kern, Brett, Weingart and Eck found that people entering multiparty negotiations held weaker fixed-pie perceptions than people negotiating in pairs.
questions.f: Kern, Brett, Weingart and Eck found that people entering multiparty negotiations held stronger fixed-pie perceptions than people negotiating in pairs.
questions.x: Across three studies and an internal meta-analysis, the fixed-pie belief was weaker when more than two parties were at the table. The false version reverses the direction of the effect; note that most of this evidence comes from simulations.

questions.t: Rehearsing a roadmap update, a manager says, "We'll launch in the [pause] third quarter, once legal [pause] signs off." Her pauses fall inside phrases, splitting words listeners need to hear as one unit.
questions.f: Rehearsing a roadmap update, a manager says, "We'll launch in the [pause] third quarter, once legal [pause] signs off." Her pauses fall at the ends of thought groups, showing listeners which words belong together.
questions.x: "In the third quarter" and "legal signs off" are each one chunk, so a silence in the middle breaks the unit. Thought-group pauses go after the chunk: "We'll launch in the third quarter / once legal signs off."

questions.t: When reporting revenue, growth and margin aloud, give each figure its own chunk with a short silent pause after it, rather than running all three together in one breath.
questions.f: When reporting revenue, growth and margin aloud, run all three figures together in one breath and pause once at the end, rather than pausing after each figure.
questions.x: A pause and slight pitch drop after each number lets listeners hear which figure goes with which measure and hold it before the next arrives. Strung together, the figures blur, which is the problem the finance example fixes.

questions.t: Inserting short pauses at phrase boundaries in radio news raised second-language listeners' comprehension, most for lower-level learners, though that result comes from a single master's thesis.
questions.f: Inserting short pauses at phrase boundaries in radio news raised second-language listeners' comprehension, most for advanced learners, though that result comes from a single master's thesis.
questions.x: Van Loon's experiment found the biggest gain for the weakest listeners, which is why chunking matters most for second-language audiences and poor connections. Being one thesis, it is suggestive rather than settled.

questions.t: A well-rested reviewer finds an error in a report a colleague wrote at the end of a 14-hour on-call shift and comments, "This is just sloppy." Reading a fatigued colleague's slip as a character flaw is the hot-cold empathy gap.
questions.f: A well-rested reviewer finds an error in a report a colleague wrote at the end of a 14-hour on-call shift and comments, "This is just sloppy." Reading a fatigued colleague's slip as a character flaw is the curse of knowledge.
questions.x: The tell is a difference in state: a calm, rested judge underestimates how much fatigue drives behaviour and blames motivation instead of circumstances. The curse of knowledge is about being unable to forget what you know, not about misjudging someone's emotional or physical state.

questions.t: When a colleague describes burnout from a release crunch you also lived through, keep the focus on her account and validate it, rather than retelling how you got through yours.
questions.f: When a colleague describes burnout from a release crunch you also lived through, start by retelling how you got through yours, since shared experience makes your support land better.
questions.x: A 2024 set of studies found that people who had endured the same distress offered compassion sufferers rated as less helpful, partly because they turned to their own story and validated less. Having been there is a warning sign, not a credential.

questions.t: In Nordgren's research, people who were not tired or in pain blamed a struggling person's poor performance on low motivation, and simply telling them to empathise did not close that gap.
questions.f: In Nordgren's research, people who were not tired or in pain blamed a struggling person's poor performance on low motivation, and simply telling them to empathise was enough to close that gap.
questions.x: A bare instruction to empathise left the cold group's judgments unchanged, which is why the advice is to ask the other person and assume their experience is worse than it looks. Awareness is a prompt to check, not a cure.

questions.t: Two engineers sort out a recurring build-config error over direct messages. A week later a third engineer asks the same question in the team channel and nobody can point to the answer. Solving it privately was a chat-etiquette mistake, because it hid the answer from the next person who needed it.
questions.f: Two engineers sort out a recurring build-config error over direct messages. A week later a third engineer asks the same question in the team channel and nobody can point to the answer. Solving it privately was good chat etiquette, because it kept the team channel free of noise.
questions.x: Direct messages suit genuinely private or one-person matters; a team problem belongs in a channel thread so the answer stays findable. The tell is the repeat question that nobody can answer from the record.

questions.t: When a chat thread about a release date has gone several rounds without agreement, move to a short call, then post the outcome back in the same thread.
questions.f: When a chat thread about a release date has gone several rounds without agreement, add an @channel alert so the whole team weighs in, then post the outcome back in the same thread.
questions.x: Chat etiquette treats a few unresolved back-and-forths, or a topic turning sensitive, as the cue to talk live. Channel-wide alerts are for urgent items the team has agreed qualify, and widening an argument adds noise rather than agreement.

questions.t: In Gloria Mark's lab experiment, people interrupted every few minutes while answering email finished faster but reported more stress and effort, because they compensated by working harder.
questions.f: In Gloria Mark's lab experiment, people interrupted every few minutes while answering email finished more slowly and reported more stress, because each interruption made them start the task over.
questions.x: Interrupted participants sped up, not down; the cost showed up as stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. That hidden cost is why chat etiquette tries to cut needless alerts. The study had 48 mostly student participants, so it is indirect support.

questions.topic: The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states
questions.t: In Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec's 1998 lying game, liars predicted about 49% of their group would catch them, but only about 26% did, roughly chance.
questions.f: In Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec's 1998 lying game, liars predicted about 26% of their group would catch them, but about 49% did, well above chance.
questions.x: Liars roughly doubled the share of the group they expected to see through them; actual detection sat near chance. The swapped version reverses the bias the study was named for.

questions.topic: The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states
questions.t: In the 1998 lying studies, silent observers who knew the same facts as each liar predicted far lower detection than the liars did, so the bias seems to come from experiencing the lie yourself.
questions.f: In the 1998 lying studies, silent observers who knew the same facts as each liar predicted detection as high as the liars did, so the bias seems to come from a general belief that lies are easy to spot.
questions.x: The yoked observers guessed around a quarter would catch the lie, versus about 44% for the liars. Living the inner state, not general beliefs about lying, inflated the estimate.

questions.topic: The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states
questions.t: Gilovich and colleagues proposed that when each bystander thinks their own alarm shows but sees everyone else looking calm, each concludes the others are unworried, so nobody steps in.
questions.f: Gilovich and colleagues proposed that when each bystander thinks their own alarm is hidden but sees everyone else looking worried, each assumes someone else will act, so nobody steps in.
questions.x: In the cheating study people felt more concerned than they looked yet believed their concern was visible. Reading others' calm faces as calm minds is the proposed route to silence; the false version reverses what each person believes about their own visibility.

questions.t: On a call with a partner office, a consultant gets the delivery date she wanted by overruling their lead in front of his own team, who stay cold for weeks afterwards. By Deardorff's test, her behaviour was effective but not appropriate.
questions.f: On a call with a partner office, a consultant gets the delivery date she wanted by overruling their lead in front of his own team, who stay cold for weeks afterwards. By Deardorff's test, her behaviour was appropriate but not effective.
questions.x: Deardorff's outcome has two parts: effective means you reached your goal, appropriate means the other side saw your conduct as acceptable. She got the date, so it was effective; the public overruling and the chill that followed show it was not appropriate.

questions.t: To gauge how your calls with a partner office are going, ask a colleague from that office how your approach lands, rather than relying on your own sense of how well you adapted.
questions.f: To gauge how your calls with a partner office are going, rate your own adaptability on a self-assessment questionnaire, rather than asking a colleague from that office how you come across.
questions.x: Self-report shows only half the picture, and tested abilities often diverge from actual behaviour, so Deardorff recommends getting the other side's view of how your conduct landed. A self-rating alone can miss exactly the misreadings that matter.

questions.t: A 2001 meta-analysis found cross-cultural training only modestly linked to adjustment (r = 0.12) and somewhat more to performance (r = 0.23).
questions.f: A 2001 meta-analysis found cross-cultural training only modestly linked to performance (r = 0.12) and somewhat more to adjustment (r = 0.23).
questions.x: The smaller correlation was with adjustment and the larger with performance; both are small, which is why reviewers favour experiential learning with reflection over one-off courses. The false version swaps the two outcomes.

questions.t: Each week an analyst mentions in stand-up that she worked late or over the weekend to finish her part. In Jones and Pittman's taxonomy she is using exemplification, aiming to look dedicated.
questions.f: Each week an analyst mentions in stand-up that she worked late or over the weekend to finish her part. In Jones and Pittman's taxonomy she is using ingratiation, aiming to look likeable.
questions.x: Advertising extra effort targets an image of dedication, which is exemplification. Ingratiation seeks to be liked, through favours or flattery; the article also notes exemplification is linked to perceptions of office politics.

questions.t: Introducing yourself at a team kickoff, offer a checkable result and a real, workable weakness, rather than a joke like "I'm probably too obsessive about detail."
questions.f: Introducing yourself at a team kickoff, open with a joke like "I'm probably too obsessive about detail," rather than offering a checkable result and a real, workable weakness.
questions.x: The joke is a humblebrag, which people judge as insincere and like less than plain bragging or honest admissions. A concrete result lets listeners judge competence themselves, and a real weakness reads as candid.

questions.t: In Barrick and colleagues' 2009 meta-analysis, impression management correlated more strongly with interview ratings (.47) than with later job performance ratings (.15).
questions.f: In Barrick and colleagues' 2009 meta-analysis, impression management correlated more strongly with later job performance ratings (.47) than with interview ratings (.15).
questions.x: Self-presentation sways interviewers far more than it shows up in later performance ratings, a warning that what impresses in an interview does not always predict performance on the job.

questions.t: Stung by a terse email copied to her manager, an engineer holds off replying but spends the hour rereading it and venting to a teammate. Her pause has become rumination, which tends to leave people angrier.
questions.f: Stung by a terse email copied to her manager, an engineer holds off replying but spends the hour rereading it and venting to a teammate. Her pause is a cooling-off period working as intended.
questions.x: What fills the gap decides whether it cools you down. Replaying the slight and venting keep the anger hot; an absorbing, unrelated task is what let anger fade in the experiments.

questions.t: When an angry message needs an answer, send a short holding line with a reply-by time, such as "I'll come back to you by 3 pm," so the delay doesn't read as silence or avoidance.
questions.f: When an angry message needs an answer, stay silent until you have fully calmed down, since any reply sent while upset, even a holding line, risks committing you to something.
questions.x: A holding line meets the need to respond without committing to a hot-state reply, and the time tells the other person when to expect the real answer. Unexplained silence can look like avoidance.

questions.t: In Oechssler, Roider and Schmitz's large online study, a 24-hour cooling-off period barely changed how often people rejected unfair offers when stakes were low, and helped only when stakes felt high.
questions.f: In Oechssler, Roider and Schmitz's large online study, a 24-hour cooling-off period sharply cut rejections of unfair offers when stakes were low, and mattered less when stakes felt high.
questions.x: This study challenges how general the cooling-off benefit is: with ordinary cash stakes the delay made little difference. A pause is useful, but not a cure-all.

questions.t: The summary page of a pricing review for the sales VP reads: "This study examined three years of deal data using regression analysis. Results indicate that discount depth is associated with churn." It is written like an academic abstract, not an executive summary.
questions.f: The summary page of a pricing review for the sales VP reads: "This study examined three years of deal data using regression analysis. Results indicate that discount depth is associated with churn." It is a sound executive summary, since it covers purpose, method and results.
questions.x: Purpose, method and results for peers is the abstract's recipe. An executive summary leads with the recommendation, frames it in the reader's terms such as revenue or risk, gives the numbers and ends with the decision needed; this one has no ask at all.

questions.t: Draft the executive summary after the full report is finished, then try it on someone from the target audience to see what they find useful.
questions.f: Draft the executive summary before writing the full report, so it can steer the analysis, then try it on someone from the target audience to see what they find useful.
questions.x: Until the analysis is done you can't name the findings or the recommendation the summary must lead with, so guides tell you to write it last. Testing it on a real reader then shows whether it stands alone.

questions.t: The Canadian Health Services Research Foundation's 1:3:25 rule asks for one page of main messages, a three-page executive summary and no more than 25 pages of findings.
questions.f: The Canadian Health Services Research Foundation's 1:3:25 rule asks for a one-page executive summary, three pages of main messages and no more than 25 pages of findings.
questions.x: In 1:3:25 the single page holds the key messages and the executive summary is the three-page middle layer, both sitting above a findings section capped at 25 pages. The false version swaps the two top layers.

questions.t: In a design review, a lead tells a junior writer her draft "looks great," then tells a peer afterwards that it was unusable. On the radical candor grid, that is manipulative insincerity.
questions.f: In a design review, a lead tells a junior writer her draft "looks great," then tells a peer afterwards that it was unusable. On the radical candor grid, that is ruinous empathy.
questions.x: Flattery to the face plus complaints behind the back is low care and low challenge: manipulative insincerity, which Scott ranks worst. Ruinous empathy softens criticism out of real care, without the backstabbing.

questions.t: To start practising radical candor with a team, first ask for criticism of yourself, such as what you could stop doing to be easier to work with, then wait out the silence and reward the honesty.
questions.f: To start practising radical candor with a team, first give each report one piece of direct criticism, so they see candor modelled before you ask for criticism of yourself.
questions.x: Scott's advice begins with soliciting feedback, not giving it; leading with criticism is how the approach slides into obnoxious aggression. Rewarding the first honest answer shows the request is real.

questions.t: Radical candor rests mainly on Kim Scott's managerial experience; a 2016 conceptual paper proposed a training intervention but said there was no empirical evidence for it yet.
questions.f: Radical candor rests on controlled studies; a 2016 paper tested the framework as a package and confirmed that its four quadrants predict how well feedback lands.
questions.x: The framework is practitioner guidance: it hasn't been tested as a package. Studies on how people overestimate the cost of honesty support its premise only indirectly.

questions.t: A designer says the client rejected her mock-ups twice this week, and her lead replies, "Twice? Last year a client rejected mine six times." That is a shift response.
questions.f: A designer says the client rejected her mock-ups twice this week, and her lead replies, "Twice? Last year a client rejected mine six times." That is a support response.
questions.x: The reply turns her news into an opening for his own story, moving attention to him. A support response would keep the topic hers, for example "Twice - what did they push back on?"

questions.t: After a conversation, roughly count your shift and support replies; if shifts dominated, open your next conversation with two support replies in a row.
questions.f: After a conversation, roughly count your shift and support replies; if shifts dominated, close your next conversation by asking whether the other person felt heard.
questions.x: The habit is fixed at the start of the next exchange, by deliberately making your first replies about their topic. Asking at the end whether they felt heard doesn't change the replies that shifted the focus.

questions.t: Charles Derber drew the shift-support distinction from more than a hundred recorded dinner conversations, in which shift responses were the more common of the two.
questions.f: Charles Derber drew the shift-support distinction from more than a hundred recorded dinner conversations, in which support responses were the more common of the two.
questions.x: Derber, a Boston College sociologist, found shift responses predominated and saw their habitual use as the core of conversational narcissism. His categories come from observation, not controlled experiments.

questions.t: Before approving a data-warehouse migration, a director asks a small sub-team to build a complete alternative plan and then has the two plans debated side by side. That is dialectical inquiry.
questions.f: Before approving a data-warehouse migration, a director asks a small sub-team to build a complete alternative plan and then has the two plans debated side by side. That is devil's advocacy.
questions.x: The tell is the full counter-plan: dialectical inquiry builds and debates a rival option. A devil's advocate instead critiques the leading proposal's assumptions, evidence and logic without having to author a whole alternative.

questions.t: When a room seems agreed on a vendor switch, name a colleague as devil's advocate, say openly that the role is assigned, and have the proposal's owner answer each of her objections before you decide.
questions.f: When a room seems agreed on a vendor switch, ask "Any objections?" and, if nobody speaks up, take the silence as a tested decision and sign the contract.
questions.x: An open call for objections in a room that already looks aligned rarely surfaces doubts. Assigning and labelling the critic role makes challenge part of the job rather than disloyalty, and forces the owner to deal with specific weaknesses before committing.

questions.t: In a 2002 experiment with employees and managers, groups that contained genuine dissenters curbed one-sided information search better than groups relying on an assigned devil's advocate.
questions.f: In a 2002 experiment with employees and managers, groups relying on an assigned devil's advocate curbed one-sided information search better than groups that contained genuine dissenters.
questions.x: Schulz-Hardt and colleagues found sincere disagreement beat role-played challenge, which is why the technique works best on top of real diversity of view. The false version reverses which form of dissent did better.

questions.t: At a quarterly review, a lead puts nine bullets in small type on each slide and reads every line aloud word for word while the leaders read along. That is death by PowerPoint: the slides carry the talk and compete with the speaker.
questions.f: At a quarterly review, a lead puts nine bullets in small type on each slide and reads every line aloud word for word while the leaders read along. That is a wall of text: one unbroken block with nothing to guide the eye.
questions.x: Crowded bullet slides read aloud verbatim are the two signature faults audiences complained about most. A wall of text is an unbroken paragraph in writing; here the problem is fragmented bullets taking over from the speaker.

questions.t: When a leadership review needs detailed ticket data, send it as a one-page handout before the meeting and keep the slides for the live argument and the ask.
questions.f: When a leadership review needs detailed ticket data, pack it into the slides so the deck doubles as the record, and skip the separate handout.
questions.x: Dense analysis reads better at the reader's own pace in a document; the Columbia board and Tufte both favoured written papers for complex reasoning. A deck meant to be both talk and record usually serves neither.

questions.t: David Farkas argued in 2006 that most faults Tufte blamed on slide software come from unskilled use and organisational culture, so bad slide habits, not slides themselves, are the problem.
questions.f: David Farkas argued in 2006 that Tufte was right that slide software itself corrupts reasoning whoever uses it, so teams should stop using slides altogether.
questions.x: Farkas challenged Tufte's stronger claim, saying it judges slides as free-standing documents and blames the tool for users' habits. The practical reading is to fix how decks are built, not to ban them.

questions.t: An interviewer asks a candidate, "A key client threatens to leave over a missed deadline. What do you do in the first 24 hours?" That is a situational question.
questions.f: An interviewer asks a candidate, "A key client threatens to leave over a missed deadline. What do you do in the first 24 hours?" That is a behavioural question.
questions.x: A situational question poses a job-like scenario to respond to; a behavioural one asks about a real past event, as in "Tell me about a time a client threatened to leave." Both work in structured interviews.

questions.t: Asked how you handle conflicting priorities in an interview, describe one real case: the situation, what you yourself did, and the result, then stop and let the interviewer probe.
