questions.f: Asked how you handle conflicting priorities in an interview, describe yourself as organised and calm under pressure, then offer a real case only if the interviewer probes.
questions.x: A concrete story with your own actions and the outcome gives the interviewer scorable evidence. A self-description like "I'm very organised" gives them nothing to rate against the benchmark.

questions.t: In Sackett, Zhang, Berry and Lievens's 2022 re-analysis, structured interviews had the highest average operational validity of the predictors they examined, about r = .42.
questions.f: In Sackett, Zhang, Berry and Lievens's 2022 re-analysis, unstructured interviews had the highest average operational validity of the predictors they examined, about r = .42.
questions.x: Structure (same job-based questions, scored against benchmarks) is what made interviews predict job performance best, though results varied widely across studies. Unstructured gut-feel interviews predict less well.

questions.t: If a leadership team is likely to resist your report's recommendation to close a site, lead with the background and evidence and reach the recommendation at the end.
questions.f: If a leadership team is likely to resist your report's recommendation to close a site, open with the recommendation in the first lines and let the evidence follow it.
questions.x: Textbook guidance ties placement to the reader's likely reaction: recommendation first for neutral or positive readers, evidence first for resistant ones so the case is built before the conclusion lands. Opening cold with an unwelcome recommendation invites rejection before the reasons are heard.

questions.t: Meeting minutes and expense reports are informational reports, presenting facts without judgement, while a feasibility study that recommends a course of action is an analytical report.
questions.f: Meeting minutes and expense reports are analytical reports, presenting facts with an interpretation, while a feasibility study that recommends a course of action is an informational report.
questions.x: Informational reports record events, activities or conditions without judgement; analytical reports add analysis to solve a problem or recommend something. The false version swaps the two families.

questions.t: A 2016 systematic review of six randomised trials found evidence summaries probably easier to understand than full reviews, but their effect on whether decision makers actually used the evidence was unclear.
questions.f: A 2016 systematic review of six randomised trials found evidence summaries probably easier to understand than full reviews, and found they clearly increased how often decision makers used the evidence.
questions.x: Petkovic and colleagues' review supports the comprehension benefit of summary-first formats, not a proven effect on decisions. The trials were also in health policy, so the transfer to ordinary business reports is plausible but untested.

questions.t: A project manager ends her request to another team with "No rush at all, whenever you get a chance, only if it's no trouble," and the fix she needs never arrives. In Spitzberg's grid of outcomes, that is sufficing.
questions.f: A project manager ends her request to another team with "No rush at all, whenever you get a chance, only if it's no trouble," and the fix she needs never arrives. In Spitzberg's grid of outcomes, that is maximizing.
questions.x: Sufficing is polite and appropriate but not effective: nobody was offended, and nothing happened. Maximizing is the opposite corner, where you get your way but break norms or bruise the relationship.

questions.t: If you know what to say to a client about a scope overrun and can say it well, yet keep postponing the call, work on the motivation component, your avoidance, rather than studying more phrasing.
questions.f: If you know what to say to a client about a scope overrun and can say it well, yet keep postponing the call, work on the knowledge component by studying more phrasing for it.
questions.x: The component model splits competence into motivation, knowledge and skill, and each needs a different fix. Knowing what fits and being able to do it, yet avoiding the interaction, points to motivation; more phrasing adds knowledge you already have.

questions.t: In a 2008 survey of 220 US employees, their rating of the supervisor's communicator competence explained about 68% of the variance in their communication satisfaction.
questions.f: In a 2008 survey of 220 US employees, their rating of the supervisor's communicator competence explained about 18% of the variance in their communication satisfaction.
questions.x: Madlock found supervisor competence accounted for roughly 68% of communication satisfaction and about 18% of job satisfaction; the false version borrows the job-satisfaction figure. The study is cross-sectional, so it shows association, not cause.

questions.t: A finance partner ends a headcount negotiation with a little less than she asked for, but says she felt heard and can defend the deal to her boss. Those feelings of subjective value predict whether she'll deal with you again better than the economic result does.
questions.f: A finance partner ends a headcount negotiation with a little less than she asked for, but says she felt heard and can defend the deal to her boss. Those feelings matter less than the economic result in predicting whether she'll deal with you again.
questions.x: Curhan, Elfenbein and Xu found feelings about the process, oneself and the relationship predicted later negotiation decisions better than economic outcomes. Feeling heard and being able to save face are exactly those clusters, so they shape the next negotiation.

questions.t: When a supplier's late delivery puts your launch at risk, say plainly that you're disappointed with the offer rather than staging anger, which can win concessions but reliably damages trust.
questions.f: When a supplier's late delivery puts your launch at risk, stage some anger at their account rep, since an angry display reliably wins concessions without much cost to the relationship.
questions.x: The 2023 review finds anger extracts concessions only under some conditions and reliably harms trust, while expressed disappointment can bring similar gains at lower cost. Displaying emotion you don't feel also shades into deception.

questions.t: ElShenawy's 2010 meta-analysis of negotiation-training experiments linked longer training with much better individual performance (r = .76) than short training (r = .22).
questions.f: ElShenawy's 2010 meta-analysis of negotiation-training experiments linked short training with much better individual performance (r = .76) than longer training (r = .22).
questions.x: The larger correlation went with longer training. These are laboratory results across 57 experiments, so they say little about long-term transfer to the job; the false version swaps which kind of training did better.

questions.t: Annoyed by a missed hand-off, an engineer fires off a chat message to a colleague far blunter than anything he would say to her face. That is the uninhibited messaging that reduced social cues make easier, and a reason to reread before sending.
questions.f: Annoyed by a missed hand-off, an engineer fires off a chat message to a colleague far blunter than anything he would say to her face. That is the status equalisation that reduced social cues make easier, and a reason to reread before sending.
questions.x: The tell is bluntness he would not use in person: with fewer cues about the person and setting, text gets less inhibited. Status equalisation is a different reduced-cues effect, about rank mattering less in who speaks up, and has nothing to do with tone.

questions.t: Lee Sproull and Sara Kiesler at Carnegie Mellon framed workplace email as a loss of social context cues, in a 1986 field study at a Fortune 500 company.
questions.f: Joseph Walther and Judee Burgoon framed workplace email as a loss of social context cues, in a 1986 field study at a Fortune 500 company.
questions.x: The cues-filtered-out framing came from Sproull and Kiesler's field study of real employee email. Walther and Burgoon came later, in 1992, and challenged that picture rather than proposing it.

questions.t: Walther and Burgoon found time mattered more than medium: computer-mediated groups grew more positive over repeated exchanges, so digital working relationships develop more slowly rather than staying colder.
questions.f: Walther and Burgoon found medium mattered more than time: computer-mediated groups stayed less positive however many exchanges they had, so digital working relationships stay colder rather than developing more slowly.
questions.x: This is the social information processing view: people carry relational meaning through wording, address and sign-offs, which takes longer in text. Their 1992 study found repeated contact closed much of the gap the cues-filtered-out view had predicted would persist.

questions.t: A developer leaves sharp comments in design docs and talks freely in one-on-ones, but says nothing in the 12-person planning meeting, especially when directors attend. That pattern points to communication apprehension about group settings.
questions.f: A developer leaves sharp comments in design docs and talks freely in one-on-ones, but says nothing in the 12-person planning meeting, especially when directors attend. That pattern points to him having little to contribute on planning.
questions.x: The tell is a split across settings: strong input in writing and one-to-one, silence where the audience is larger and higher status, both of which raise apprehension. His written comments show he has plenty to add.

questions.t: To help apprehensive colleagues contribute, a facilitator can share the questions before the meeting and use rounds, small groups or written input instead of relying on the open floor.
questions.f: To help apprehensive colleagues contribute, a facilitator can rely on the open floor and call on quiet people without warning, so they get practice speaking up.
questions.x: Uncertainty, novelty and audience size all raise apprehension, so advance questions and structured or written routes lower the cost of contributing. Surprise cold-calls add exactly the uncertainty that makes it worse.

questions.t: Communication apprehension is broader than stage fright: McCroskey's PRCA-24 scores it separately for group discussion, meetings, one-to-one conversation and public speaking.
questions.f: Communication apprehension is another name for stage fright: McCroskey's PRCA-24 scores it as anxiety about public speaking, with no separate settings.
questions.x: The measure covers four settings and adds them into a total, and the subscores show where someone's apprehension sits so practice can target it. Public-speaking anxiety is just its best-known form.

questions.t: An HR lead proposes buying software that scores job candidates' emotions from their faces on recorded video interviews. That is the kind of high-stakes judgement the 2019 Barrett review warned against basing on facial analysis.
questions.f: An HR lead proposes buying software that scores job candidates' emotions from their faces on recorded video interviews. That is the kind of high-stakes judgement the 2019 Barrett review said facial analysis can now support.
questions.x: The review found that a given expression maps to a given feeling too loosely and inconsistently to infer emotion from the face alone, and named hiring among the uses to avoid. Faces are cues to check, not verdicts to score.

questions.t: On a video call, make your nods, smiles and raised eyebrows a little larger than you would in person, so colleagues can see on a small tile that you are following.
questions.f: On a video call, make your nods, smiles and raised eyebrows a little smaller than you would in person, since the camera exaggerates every reaction on a small tile.
questions.x: A resting face on a small video tile is easily read as disengaged, so deliberate, slightly enlarged reactions help others see you are listening. Shrinking them makes the misreading more likely, not less.

questions.t: In Cowen, Keltner and colleagues' 2021 study of about 6 million videos, 16 kinds of facial expression were tied to similar social contexts, with about 70% of those links preserved across 12 world regions.
questions.f: In Cowen, Keltner and colleagues' 2021 study of about 6 million videos, 16 kinds of facial expression were tied to different social contexts, with only about 20% of those links preserved across 12 world regions.
questions.x: The study supports some cross-cultural regularity in when expressions occur, though how often each appeared varied by region. That partial support is why the article lands on contested rather than debunked or settled.

questions.topic: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance
questions.t: Pooling 607 effect sizes, Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis put the average effect of feedback interventions on performance at d = 0.41, a moderate gain.
questions.f: Pooling 607 effect sizes, Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis put the average effect of feedback interventions on performance at d = 0.91, a very large gain.
questions.x: The average was moderate, d = 0.41, and hid wide spread, with many interventions hurting performance. A very large average would not fit the study's message that feedback often backfires.

questions.topic: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance
questions.t: In Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis, feedback interventions paired with goal setting had stronger effects on performance, while those carrying praise had weaker ones.
questions.f: In Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis, feedback interventions carrying praise had stronger effects on performance, while those paired with goal setting had weaker ones.
questions.x: Goals keep attention on the task, which strengthens feedback; praise pulls attention toward the self and dilutes it. So give feedback with a concrete target, such as two days instead of four next quarter.

questions.topic: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance
questions.t: Kluger and DeNisi showed that harmful effects of feedback had been reported since the early 1900s but were routinely explained away, partly because influential reviews treated feedback as reliably helpful.
questions.f: Kluger and DeNisi showed that harmful effects of feedback were first reported in the late 1980s, shortly before their review, because earlier studies had never measured them.
questions.x: Their historical review found the negative effects were old news, dismissed for decades because reviews such as Ammons' 1956 summary assumed feedback always helps. The false version invents a late discovery.

questions.t: Choosing between two vendors, a team spends forty minutes on the pricing everyone saw in the deck, and the security engineer's knowledge of a failed audit never comes up. That is the hidden-profile problem: discussion favours shared information over what one person holds.
questions.f: Choosing between two vendors, a team spends forty minutes on the pricing everyone saw in the deck, and the security engineer's knowledge of a failed audit never comes up. That is production blocking: only one person can talk at a time.
questions.x: The tell is that the time went to facts all members already knew while one member's unique fact stayed hidden, which is the bias hidden-profile research documents. Production blocking describes ideas lost while people wait their turn in brainstorming, not a pull toward shared facts.

questions.t: Before a team chooses between two rollout plans, go round each function and ask what it knows about the options that the others might not, so gaps in the pooled information become visible.
questions.f: Before a team chooses between two rollout plans, ask the room once whether anyone has concerns, and treat a quiet room as a sign the relevant information has been shared.
questions.x: Unique information is what predicts good group decisions, and a general call for concerns lets it stay hidden. Asking each person explicitly what they hold that others lack is the step the board-study authors recommend.

questions.t: In Schulz-Hardt and colleagues' 2006 study, three-person groups that began by disagreeing found the hidden best option far more often, even when none of them had started out favouring it.
questions.f: In Schulz-Hardt and colleagues' 2006 study, three-person groups that began by disagreeing found the hidden best option far more often, but only when at least one of them had started out favouring it.
questions.x: Prior dissent helped even when every member's first choice was wrong, because disagreement drives deeper discussion of the information. That is why collecting views independently first and valuing dissent beats smoothing it over.

questions.t: A product manager's eight-page vendor review goes to a director who will skim it, with headings "Overview", "Findings", "Discussion" and "Next steps". These are label headings: each could sit on any document, so the director must open every section to learn its point.
questions.f: A product manager's eight-page vendor review goes to a director who will skim it, with headings "Overview", "Findings", "Discussion" and "Next steps". These are informative headings: each tells the director what kind of content sits below it.
questions.x: Saying what kind of content a section holds is exactly what a label does. An informative heading states the section's point, such as the finding or the decision needed, so the headings alone tell the story.

questions.t: In a decision paper for a busy director, write statement headings such as "Cutting to 400 seats saves $90K a year" rather than questions such as "How much could we save?"
questions.f: In a decision paper for a busy director, write question headings such as "How much could we save?" rather than statements such as "Cutting to 400 seats saves $90K a year"
questions.x: A question heading puts the key idea at the end and withholds your answer, which slows a scanning reader who wants your conclusion. Questions suit FAQs and public pages where you know what people will ask.

questions.t: In Lorch and Lorch's 1996 experiments, headings improved readers' recall of unfamiliar topics but not of familiar ones.
questions.f: In Lorch and Lorch's 1996 experiments, headings improved readers' recall of familiar topics but not of unfamiliar ones.
questions.x: Headings helped most where readers had no prior map of the subject, which is why they matter for newcomers and outsiders. Readers who already knew a topic recalled it about as well without them.

questions.t: Needing a vice president's sign-off on the mockups, a designer posts in a shared channel, "Still no sign-off on the mockups," and hopes he takes the hint. She has gone off record, a strategy a senior reader can simply miss.
questions.f: Needing a vice president's sign-off on the mockups, a designer posts in a shared channel, "Still no sign-off on the mockups," and hopes he takes the hint. She has used negative politeness, hedging her request to respect his autonomy.
questions.x: A hint that never states the ask is the off-record strategy; negative politeness still makes the request, softened with hedges, questions or apologies ("Would you be able to sign off by Friday?"). With higher-status readers, make the actual ask recoverable.

questions.t: When you must criticise a peer's analysis, redress the threat to her positive face, for instance by naming what she got right, rather than apologising as if you were imposing on her time.
questions.f: When you must criticise a peer's analysis, apologise as if you were imposing on her time, rather than redressing the threat to her positive face by naming what she got right.
questions.x: Experiments suggest a strategy reads as most polite when it repairs the kind of face the act endangers. Criticism threatens the wish to be valued, so approval fits it; an apology suits a request that imposes on someone's freedom.

questions.t: In a large study of online requests, Wikipedia editors wrote more politely before winning administrator elections and less politely afterwards, matching the prediction that power lowers politeness.
questions.f: In a large study of online requests, Wikipedia editors wrote less politely before winning administrator elections and more politely afterwards, matching the prediction that power raises politeness.
questions.x: Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil and colleagues found politeness dropped once editors gained status, and lower-reputation Stack Exchange users were more polite than high-reputation ones. The false version reverses the direction of the power effect.

questions.t: A manager asks a report, "Would you be willing to send the weekly numbers by Thursday noon?" When she mentions a clash, he says a slip will show up in her review. In NVC terms, he made a demand.
questions.f: A manager asks a report, "Would you be willing to send the weekly numbers by Thursday noon?" When she mentions a clash, he says a slip will show up in her review. In NVC terms, he made a request.
questions.x: NVC's test is what happens after a "no": if declining is punished, it was a demand, however politely it was phrased. A real request stays open to her answer and explores other ways to meet the need.

questions.t: Before raising late plan changes with a colleague, name your need, such as being able to stand behind what the client sees, separately from the one fix you prefer, so other solutions stay open.
questions.f: Before raising late plan changes with a colleague, state the one fix you prefer as your need, so the colleague knows exactly what would satisfy you and the talk stays short.
questions.x: NVC keeps a need free of any particular person or action; folding your preferred strategy into the need closes off other ways to meet it. Name the value first, then make one concrete request.

questions.t: A 2024 scoping review found only seven studies of NVC in health-care work, just two of them experimental, so claims that NVC reliably resolves workplace conflict outrun the data.
questions.f: A 2024 scoping review found consistent results across dozens of randomised trials of NVC in health-care work, establishing it as a reliable way to resolve workplace conflict.
questions.x: The evidence for NVC is encouraging but thin: few, small, mostly non-experimental studies and no large workplace trials. Treat it as a useful discipline, not a proven conflict cure.

questions.t: At kickoff, an HR director asks the analytics team to "make the onboarding report better" but can't say what better would look like. In Ojasalo's terms that is a fuzzy expectation, which the team should turn into a precise, checkable goal before building anything.
questions.f: At kickoff, an HR director asks the analytics team to "make the onboarding report better" but can't say what better would look like. In Ojasalo's terms that is an implicit expectation, which the team should turn into a precise, checkable goal before building anything.
questions.x: Fuzzy means the client wants an improvement without knowing what it is, which is what happens here. An implicit expectation is a specific want the client assumes and never voices, such as expecting mobile access without mentioning it; both need surfacing, but they are different problems.
